Scottish bacteriologist Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in September 1928 at St Mary's Hospital in London. The date usually given is 28 September 1928, though some accounts give 15 September [1][2]. He saw that a Penicillium mould had contaminated a culture plate of Staphylococcus bacteria, and the bacteria around the mould were dying. He worked out that a substance released by the mould was killing them and named it "penicillin" [1][3]. Fleming couldn't purify it in useful amounts. In the late 1930s and 1940s, Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain's team at Oxford turned it into a drug that could be used and mass-produced. All three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine [1][3].
